study.title: Exodus 31 - Ability granted by God, the holiness of the sabbath, and the tables of the testimony
study.overview: Exodus 31 contains the long speech of the LORD to Moses in Mount Sinai. The chapter unites three inseparable themes: God calls and empowers artisans for the work of the tabernacle; God reaffirms the Sabbath as a sign of the covenant and mark of sanctification; and God gives Moses the tables of testimony, written by God Himself. The text shows that the worship of Israel depended not only on materials and techniques, but on divine initiative, obedience to the covenant and the authority of the word of written God.

outline.title: God calls and empowers the workers of the tabernacle
outline.explanation: The LORD names Bezalel and also associates Aoliab with him. Artistic skill is not presented as merely human talent, but as a gift of the Spirit of God to accurately perform the ordained work. The goal is to do everything according to the commandment received.

outline.title: The list of the work shows the centrality of the cult
outline.explanation: The sequence lists the tabernacle, the ark, the mercy seat, the table, the candlestick, the altars, the sink, the priestly garments, the anointing oil and the incense. The repetition of details emphasizes that the cult should follow exactly what God determined, without improvisation of human.

outline.title: The Sabbath as a sign of the covenant and the gift of the boards
outline.explanation: God reaffirms the Sabbath as a perpetual sign between Him and Israel, linked to the sanctification of the people and to rest after six days of work. The chapter ends with the surrender of the two tablets of stone, a testimony written by God Himself, at the close of the speech at Sinai.

study.context: The chapter takes place in the context of Moses" stay on Mount Sinai, at the end of the forty days and forty nights mentioned in the tradition of the book. The text also presupposes the life of Israel in the desert and the organization of the tabernacle as the center of the worship of the covenant people. Nothing in the chapter requires historical reconstructions beyond that.
study.theology: Exodus 31 teaches that God not only commands his work, but also grants the gifts necessary to execute it. The empowerment of the Spirit of God on Bezalel and the wisdom given to other craftsmen show that excellence in sacred service is a gift, not a reason for self-reliance. The chapter also presents the Sabbath as a distinct sign of the covenant: it identifies the people as belonging to the Lord, remembers that God is the one who sanctifies and teaches his practical dependence. So work and rest do not compete; both belong to obedience. Finally, the stone tablets written by God's finger reinforce the divine authority of the covenant: the covenant is not born of human initiative, but is revealed, recorded and sealed by God Himself.

scholarViews.insight: The text emphasizes that God chooses and enables those who will perform the work of the tabernacle; the ability comes from the Spirit of God for tasks that exceed normal skill.
The commentary sees the appointment of the artisans as necessary because God ordered an excellent work, but also provided the workers able to carry it out.
Bezalel's indication is understood as a special appointment to oversee the whole work, and his name is treated as significant in relation to God's protection.

questions: What changes in the way we serve when we recognize that gifts and abilities come from God to accomplish his work?
Why does the Sabbath appear as a sign of covenant and not just as a rule of rest?
How does the exact order of the construction of the tabernacle confront our tendency to adapt worship to our preference?
study.practice: Read his work and his routine in the light of this chapter: ask God for wisdom to serve faithfully, practice a real rhythm of rest consecrated to him, and treat worship as an obedient answer to his Word, not as a space for improvisation centered on himself. If you exercise leadership or ministry, value people with different gifts and recognize that God's work requires training received, not just human effort.
study.uncertainty: The text provided from Matthew Henry's notes at 31:12 is truncated, so the synthesis was made there only with the excerpt available. Nor is it possible to affirm more historical details of the tabernacle than the chapter itself and the notes explicitly say.
